awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: Research: Stigma of mental health conditions in engineering and its relationship with help-seeking attitudes of undergraduates and early professionals
awd_abstract_narration:
The last decade has seen a rise in the mental health needs of college students, with an increasing prevalence of Mental Health Conditions (MHCs) such as depression, panic disorders, and generalized anxiety among many others. Stigma, a strong feeling of disapproval, of MHCs is a society-wide issue that tends to conflict with help-seeking attitudes of those having MHCs. Engineering is known as a demanding field, where a culture of high stress and endurance is often promoted, with specific challenges to socialization, especially for members of marginalized groups. These factors tend to be linked to the onset and persistence of MHCs. Nevertheless, it is known that while engineering students do not have a higher prevalence of MHCs, those that have them are less prone to seek help than those in other professional areas. This project will explore elements of the engineering culture that may reinforce stigmatized views of MHCs, therefore limiting the ability of students and early professionals to seek help when they need it. This study will explore the experiences of students and early professionals to understand elements of the engineering culture that influence their internalized stigma, interest to learn about MHCs, and ability to help others. The project team will pay attention to students' interactions with other actors such as faculty and administrators to explore how the beliefs about MHCs are perpetuated in engineering education spaces. This study has the potential to bring valuable insights into professional cultures and how they interact with the prevalence and management of MHCs, such as key dynamics, contexts, and interactions that might promote negative views of MHCs.

The goal of this project is to identify elements of engineering culture that influence the stigma of MHCs and consequently affect the help-seeking attitudes of students and early professionals. This will be achieved through a three-year longitudinal sequential mixed methods study. Each year the relationship between the stigma of MHCs and help-seeking attitudes will be measured quantitatively through a survey with established instruments. The results of the first-year survey will be analyzed under the principles of maximum variability to inform our longitudinal multi-case study that will use thematic and narrative analyses. The longitudinal quantitative analysis will examine the evolution of the considered relationships through the years of the participants’ engineering training and transition to professional life, and how they are moderated by their characteristics, perceptions of engineering culture, engineering identity, and sense of belonging. This longitudinal approach will explore the important transition point where engineering students leave academic spaces to engage in their first professional experiences and its impact on their mental well being. The research design will also enable the study of how the outlook of students without MHCs evolves through time. Since MHCs can develop at any point in life and many elements of college life, including those specific to engineering training, have been linked to poor mental health outcomes, the result of this project have the potential to identify elements from learning and practicing engineering that could contribute to the onset of MHCs. Project results will contribute to advancing equity and inclusion in engineering through the comprehensive description of the challenges experienced by students and early professionals with MHCs. Since engineering students and professionals with other marginalized identities in engineering are more likely to experience MHCs, project results will have the potential to illustrate the specific challenges navigated by such groups. A partnership with the National Alliance of Mental Illness (NAMI) will enable a national reach of audiences in and out universities that will be supported through some of their established initiatives.

por.por_cntn:
The U.S. faces a shortage of engineers that has been projected to worsens over time. This shortage threatens the country’s long-term competitiveness.  While the reasons for such shortage are varied, the most critical are related to the lack of ability to retain students in engineering once they select it in college. Previous research has identified engineering culture as a challenge for students’ retention due to its exclusionary nature, with stress being a strong element that characterizes the undergraduate experience often affecting the mental health of students. As new generations of students become more aware of the critical role of mental health and prioritizes their own well-being it is critical that we understand the different dynamics in engineering culture that can negatively affect their experience in engineering education and potentially thwart their intentions to persist. Our project focused on further understanding such dynamics, at the intersection of stigma of mental health conditions and engineering culture and how they affect help seeking of engineering students and early professionals.

We collected quantitative data through surveys measuring students’ help-seeking, engineering specific stigma levels of mental health conditions, and perceptions of engineering identity and engineering culture, and qualitative data through interviews at two institutions in the continental U.S. yearly for three years. Our analysis of quantitative data showed that engineering-specific stigma was negatively correlated with help-seeking attitudes of students, and a more complex relationship with engineering identity. The more students identified as engineers or as belonging in engineering the less likely they were to seek help for their mental health challenges. When exploring how mental health conditions were distributed among students in the study, we found that women and other gender minorities were more highly affected by such conditions. In our analysis of data across the years, we found no significant changes through time for most stigma and help-seeking measures, but our sample showed significant increases in engineering identity and belonging through time.

We also conducted a person-based analysis using Latent Profile Analysis which identified a six-profile solution with profiles ranging from “Thriving,” characterized by strong wellbeing and supportive environments, to “Self-Reliant,” marked by high psychological distress and low belonging despite relatively positive help-seeking attitudes. These findings demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in engineering students’ mental health experiences and highlight the importance of situating wellbeing within disciplinary and institutional contexts. Implications for engineering education include the need for targeted, context-sensitive intervention that address both individual help-seeking behaviors and departmental climate.

In our qualitative analyses we found that several elements of engineering culture negatively affected students’ mental health and willingness to seek help, including an emphasis on independent problem-solving, efficiency, competition, heavy workloads, and exclusionary norms. Our results suggest that these pressures led many students to manage mental health challenges alone, view help-seeking as inefficient or weak, struggle to communicate their needs, and experience isolation, stigma, and normalized overwork; women and students of color faced additional barriers related to stereotypes, underrepresentation, and belonging. To address these issues, we recommended reframing mental health as a complex sociotechnical challenge, treating communication as a core engineering competency, reducing competitive and “weed-out” practices, expanding cooperative and collaborative learning, rejecting narratives that present poor mental health as necessary for success, and revising course and program cultures to create more inclusive support structures. Overall, our findings highlight the need for intentional cultural change in engineering education so that mental health, inclusion, and help-seeking are recognized as integral to engineering student success.

Putting them together, our results highlight a need for engineering education environments to keep intentionally reshaping narratives that reduce stigma of mental health conditions and promote more positive holistic views of engineering. Enabling engineering education and practice to support the success of a wider range of individuals.
